The mathmetician was diagnosed with cervical cancer six years ago

Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer.

The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently took part in the second season of the Celebrity Traitors, said cancerous cells were discovered after she attended a cervical screening in 2020.

She underwent a hysterectomy, describing the experience to BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs as "horrific".

"As awful as that was, it had a full stop at the end of the sentence," the 42-year-old added. "I had my five-year clear the other day. I feel so unbelievably lucky."

In Sunday's episode, Fry told show host Lauren Laverne that she had delayed a cervical screening examination for months in 2020. After she attended one, the results "didn't come back for a few weeks," she said.

"Then I got a call from my GP telling me they needed me to come back and do another test, and they did a biopsy.

"I was trying hard not to panic but when they found it was in the lymphatic system… that was when it really started to come down."

The broadcaster said she was told that her chances of survival depended on the cancerous cells not having spread to her lymph nodes, although it was not clear "how bad it was at that point".

"It's all about, basically, how far into your lymphatic system has it got. If it had not got into any lymph nodes, then the odds were in my favour and I had a really good chance of survival," she said.

Fry explained that this meant "if it was in one it would drop to a 60% chance of survival and two – the odds would go against me and it would be a 40% chance".

Fry attended a Cancer Research UK reception hosted by the King and Queen at St James's Palace in June

While in isolation in hospital following her hysterectomy, Fry said a surgeon told her that four of her lymph nodes had appeared enlarged.

She added: "I was in this hospital bed on my own and no-one could come and visit me for over a week, with nothing but the sheer terrifying drop of the end of my existence in front of me – it was horrific."

Fry described not being able to "think back to happy things that... have already happened because it is sad", while also not being able to "look forward to things you are hopeful about because it doesn't feel like it is there".

She also said she asked her then husband to set up FaceTime in the corner of a room so she could watch their two young daughters play while she was in hospital.

"I didn't want them to see me, it was too much," she said.

But she added: "Going through something like that I don't think I would swap it.

"I think it was honestly such a gift to have that experience when you're 36 and then come out the other side of it."

The presenter grew up in a working-class family and studied mathematics at University College London.

She later completed a PhD in fluid dynamics, and last year became Cambridge University's first professor of the public understanding of mathematics.

Fry has fronted BBC science series including The Future with Hannah Fry and The Secret Genius of Modern Life.

She was banished in the latest series of The Celebrity Traitors after being exposed as a traitor.

Holly Humberstone says she was having an identity crisis on a weekly basis

You might know her as a pop star, endorsed by everyone from Taylor Swift to Sam Fender, but Holly Humberstone has a secret double life.

In her spare time, the singer-songwriter is literally a cat burglar.

"We've stolen one of our neighbours' cats by accident," she laughs, in a Zoom call from her fixer-upper in New Cross, south-east London.

"He's a tiny little black cat who's come into our garden and simply chosen us."

Under the slightest scrutiny, however, her story crumbles like a biscuit in a hot cup of tea.

"OK, we've been coercing him into the house with treats," she admits. "He's just so cute.

"But we're not trying to keep him. We literally push him out every night."

Humberstone's excuse for this feline felony is that, last year, her parents sold her childhood home in Lincolnshire , external and moved to Wales – taking her pets with them.

One, a cat called Tsuki, had even been immortalised in the song Lucy as a confidante who listens to her problems but "never judges".

"Oh, she knows some secrets!" laughs the singer. "I'm so glad she can't talk."

"We actually tried to bring her to London with us, but she's a countryside cat and she hated it so much. We had to send her to Wales where she can be free and frolic."

Her parents' relocation was disruptive for the human Humberstones, too.

Their house, a "freezing cold, falling down" property 20 minutes outside of Grantham, played a huge part in the singer's success.

Her early EPs were all written there, inspiring the "wonky sonics" of her indie-leaning pop sound. The 2021 single Haunted House is even dedicated to the "friendly" spirits who inhabited the property.

"It's a place I always felt I could go back to, to remind myself of who I am," she says.

Instead, she spent 2025 "packing up 23 years of stuff my family and I had accumulated", from her old ballet shoes and poetry books to forgotten bits of jewellery.

The singer shared photos of her old bedroom, and the artefacts she'd rediscovered, while clearing out her parents' "haunted house" in Grantham (pictured, left).

The process was unsettling. Already grappling with the idea of leaving childhood behind, Humberstone found herself literally throwing away her past.

"I felt uprooted. I was having some sort of identity crisis almost weekly," she says.

So she did what she's always done, and poured those feelings into her second album, Cruel World, which entered the UK charts at number four earlier this year.

"Writing these songs felt like building myself a little shield and a kind of safety bubble," she says. "There's an escapist, fantasy element to so much of the album."

Maybe that's true, but Humberstone has always had the ability to locate a song's emotional core, and the lyrics on Cruel World don't disappoint.

" To lose somebody is to know you're only human, honey, " she sings on To Love Somebody , external , soothing her elder sister as she endures an agonising break-up.

Undeterred by that heartbreak, she throws herself headfirst into a new affair on Die Happy , external , declaring: " Hit the gas, I want it fast, want it reckless ."

But the most revealing song is the closing track, Beauty Pageant , external .

Fragile and raw, it's the sound of Humberstone in her dressing room, addressing the woman in the mirror who'd "die for the applause" but who struggles with the impossible beauty standards imposed on female artists.

Humberstone's biggest songs include Falling Asleep At The Wheel, The Walls Are Way Too Thin, Die Happy and Scarlett

"That's a song that I wasn't really setting out to write," she confesses.

"Writing about other people often feels easier than turning the magnifying glass on yourself."

The lyrics, she says, draw on a "very specific" mindset she acquired at her all-girls school in Grantham.

"It was drilled into me: You're all in competition. You're only rewarded if you're the best. And if you're not, you're worthless."

The experience "really warped the way I view other girls", she says.

Musical success made it worse. After winning the Brits Rising Star award in 2022 , Humberstone found herself competing with megastars, even though her music leaned towards the alternative side of pop.

"I'm a very small fish and I recognise that, but suddenly I was in meetings being compared to all these people on my label's roster, who are on a completely different scale," she says.

"It's something I really, really struggled with in the early days and it's something I've really had to unlearn."

Nowadays, Humberstone has stopped benchmarking herself against her peers, recognising that the need for validation never fades.

"I don't think that there's a point I could get to, or an award that I could win, where these feelings would disappear," she says.

"Everybody feels like they've still got something to prove, so I'm done with setting myself goals - because then I lose sight of the real reason that I'm doing this, which is to write music that represents me, and have other people feel understood through that music."

"I pray that one day I'll turn and face the mirror with a smile," sings Humberstone

That mindset comes to fruition in the new, expanded edition of Cruel World, whose five new songs were largely written after the original album was handed in.

"I was super proud of Cruel World and, when you've got that in your back pocket, there's room to experiment and break some of your usual parameters."

The new tracks find Humberstone embracing a new persona – more confident, more flirtatious, a little salty – with music inspired by a playlist featuring Abba, Madonna and Robyn.

The single Too Cute To Be Lonely , external is a will-they/won't-they story set at a house party.

" Don't leave a girl upset, in such a pretty dress ," she teases the object of her affections.

Terminally Yours takes place a couple of weeks later, when Humberstone realises she's fallen head-over-heels in love.

" Your stupid face is my sorry fate ," she harrumphs, cross at herself. " For [expletive]'s sake, I'm in love ."

Silver Sky, a gorgeous acoustic ballad, tells another side of the story, as she settles into her lover's arms and drifts into blissful reverie.

"I wrote that on a kind of Hail Mary trip, seeing what fell out of the air in Nashville," she reveals.

"We went over to [co-writer Maddie Diaz's] house, took a guitar into the garden and wrote Silver Sky outside, while all of these gorgeous red cardinals were singing around us.

"I usually write a lot about my mental health struggles, but I was just in the mood to write something that made me feel good."

Humberstone won the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, joining the ranks of former winners such as Sam Fender, Florence + The Machine and Adele

Not that her mental health issues are in the rear view mirror. Humberstone admits her stage nerves have only intensified since the release of Cruel World.

"It's the proudest I've been of any of my work and, for that reason, I struggled with shows because I felt a lot of pressure to go out and deliver it to the standard that I think people are expecting.

"But on the other hand, it's totally fine if you mess up or sing a wrong note. People can't connect to a pop star that feels too robotic and polished.

"So maybe my strength is that vulnerability, and I need to recognise that more."

That vulnerability has won Humberstone millions of fans, even if a hit single has (so far) eluded her.

And her audience keeps growing. In May this year, her breakout single Falling Asleep At The Wheel was awarded a silver disc... five years after its release, indicating that her songs have staying power in an era of disposable hits.

Astonishingly, this is news to Humberstone, who learns about the accolade during our interview. But it helps to clarify a thought that's been knocking around her head.

"If I'm going to be doing this for years to come, I've just got to keep making music that feels right, trusting my gut and realising there's no end point," she says.

"Reaching an end point would mean I've 'made it', but I think, maybe, that's a myth that doesn't really exist."

When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.

They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.

"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.

But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.

This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.

Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.

Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.

After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.

"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.

The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.

Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga uses his book to help convince sceptics that Ebola is real

The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.

After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.

Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.

This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.

After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.

This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.

"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.

Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.

He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.

Dr Kamwanga's mother says his experience has helped dispel some of the misinformation she had heard about Ebola

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.

"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.

In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.

Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.

"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.

Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.

The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.

However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

'I buried my parents one day after the other' - Ebola mourners learn how to grieve safely

"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.

For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.

He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.

Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.

"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.

They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.

Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.

After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.

"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."

During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.

But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.

Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.

"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".

He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.

But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.

Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.

He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."

He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing .

"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.

The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.

Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.

"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletes

Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.

That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.

The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.

But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.

Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.

More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.

Teddy Riner's video has attracted 14.5 million views on Instagram alone

Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.

So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?

"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro.

"But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."

For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.

But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.

The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.

So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.

Hard-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leads the polls in the race to be France's next president

It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.

Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"

In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.

All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices.

"People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said.

"Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."

It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers.

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?

France's Marine Le Pen, fighting court conviction and running for presidency

But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.

What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?

In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?

Protesters have for weeks taken to the streets in France over wages, the cost of living and public services

Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.

In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.

The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.

Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.

The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.

President Emmanuel Macron is among the few politicians who appears genuinely pleased by Riner's decision to run

The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.

So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.

The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".

That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.

Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".

Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat.

In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".

If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form.

In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach.

"I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering.

Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar.

Customers likened the contents of Kim Kardashian's Skims calendar to something you would find down the back of a sofa

This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa.

Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use.

"I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid."

Julia, 39, says she thinks fragrance calendars are usually good value for money

Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated.

High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight.

And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows , external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out.

But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier.

"I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist.

She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product.

"For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales."

Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist, says the calendars "serve the purpose of allowing me to try out different products"

Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice.

"I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items.

"And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy."

Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, is less keen on the calendars and says they leave consumers "bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items"

Jessica Jasper, a marketing consultant, is more positive - she thinks it's worth it. But she also thinks some companies are just jumping on a trend and that "some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing".

So can beauty calendars offer value for both the brands and the customer - an example of a win-win? Or are they mainly designed to make us spend more at Christmas than we need to?

"Some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing," says marketing consultant Jessica Jasper

Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and beauty expert, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them.

"Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous.

"But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it."

This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it.

In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do.

"The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says.

James Garner played as a substitute against Croatia on Thursday, while Jarrad Branthwaite and Josh King were unused

England manager Thomas Tuchel has omitted Josh King, James Garner and Jarrad Branthwaite from his squad to face world champions Spain in Madrid on Sunday night.

England travelled to Spain with a squad of 26 players but Uefa rules state that only 23 players can be selected in a matchday squad for Nations League games

The return to fitness of Ezri Konsa and Djed Spence - who missed Thursday's win over Croatia - has been a contributing factor in the trio's omission.

Arsenal defender Konsa could come straight back into the starting XI while James Trafford will replace Jordan Pickford in goal.

Garner replaced Declan Rice in the 77th minute of the 2-1 victory over Croatia at Wembley, scoring a goal that was subsequently disallowed, while Everton team-mate Branthwaite and Fulham's King were unused substitutes.

King received his first senior call-up for the two final Nations League fixtures in Group A3, but the midfielder, 19, will not feature in this international window.

However, fellow first-time call-ups Jobe Bellingham and James Hill are included.

Arsenal defender Ben White, who was booed when he came on as a substitute against Croatia, is also part of the reduced 23-man party.

England sit three points behind Spain in their group and know that a win will secure top spot in the table, as they already have a superior goal difference to their opponents.

Tuchel's side are already guaranteed a quarter-final spot and a first-place finish will secure them a tie against one of the runners-ups in one of the three other groups in League A.

The two-legged quarter-finals will be played in March, with semi-finals and a final to be played in June.

In the build-up to Sunday's fixture, Tuchel reminded his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocols, with the match to be the national team's first in the Spanish capital since a notorious game at Real Madrid's Bernabeu stadium in 2004 which was overshadowed by racist chanting aimed at England players.

The Spanish federation was fined last month and ordered to play their next friendly match with a partial stadium closure after fans sang "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt.

"We had the same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]," Tuchel said. "There is a protocol in place.

"Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]."

The England coach's comments were dismissed by Spain coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

Icyitonderwa : Iyi nkuru irimo amakuru ashobora kubabaza cyangwa guhungabanya bamwe mu bayisoma

Hari mu gitondo cya kare cyo mu kwezi kwa 6 muri 2024, Bas yaparitse imodoka ye iruhande rw'imodoka ifite aho kuryama (campervan) y'ababyeyi be, yari iparitse ku ku cyambu hari akazuba, mu majyaruguru y'u Buholandi.

Se na nyina, Jan na Els, bari bamaze hafi ubuzima bwabo bwose bw'abashakanye ku mazi. Ubu, ubwo bari bageze mu kigero cy'imyaka 70, ntibari bagishoboye kwita ku nzu yabo yo mu bwato. Imodoka yabo yo guturamo, yari iparitse hafi y'ubwato bunini n'ubwato buto, ni cyo kintu cyiza cyakurikiragaho.

Jan na Els binjiye mu modoka y'umuhungu wabo, Bas arayatsa. Icyo cyaje kuba igihe cya nyuma atwaye ababyeyi be mu rugendo urwo ari rwo rwose. Kuri Jan na Els, uru rugendo ni rwo rwaje kuba urwnyuma mu buzima bwabo.

Saa yine n'igice za mu gitondo (10:30), ni ho abaganga bategerzwa kubaha imiti ituma bapfa, maze bagapfira hamwe mu buryo buzwi mu Buholandi nka duo-euthanasia (gufasha abantu babiri gupfa ku bushake icyarimwe).

Ibi byemewe n'amategeko ariko ntibikunze kubaho, gusa buri mwaka Abaholandi benshi bagenda bahitamo kurangiza ubuzima bwabo muri ubu buryo.

Hasigaye iminsi itatu ngo bagere ku munsi bari bateganyije gupfiraho muri ibyo bitaro, Jan na Els bagiranye ikiganiro na BBC bari mu modoka yabo yo guturamo. Jan yari amaze igihe kinini abana n'ububabare budashira, bwari ingaruka z'imyaka myinshi yari amaze atwara imizigo mu nzira z'amazi zo mu gihugu cy'u Buholandi. Els we yari yarasanzwemo indwara yo kwibagirwa no kwangirika k'ubwonko (dementia). Inkuru yabo yakwirakwiye hirya no hino ku isi, abantu benshi bayivugaho.

Ubu, nyuma y'imyaka irenga ibiri, uno mwana wabo w'ikinege aravuga uko yagerageje kumvisha se na nyina gusubika umunsi bari bahisemo gupfira, ariko na none yashyigikiraga icyemezo cyabo cyo kutongera gukomeza kubaho. Aragaragaza umutwaro ukomeye mu marangamutima icyemezo cy'ababyeyi be cyamushyizeho, ndetse n'irungu rikomeye ryakurikiye urupfu rwabo.

Bas yari yateguye inzira nziza yo kunyuramo ajyana ababyeyi be kuri icyo kigo, ku buryo bari kubona ibyatsi bibisi byo mu rwuri n'imiyoboro y'amazi yo mu gace ka Friesland.

Agira ati: "Ndacyibuka urugendo rwose uko rwagenze." Nyina yari yicaye inyuma, naho se yicaye iruhande rwe. Mu ntangiriro baraganiraga. Els yasaga n'uwari wiyemeje kandi adashidikanya ku cyemezo cyabo cyo guhitamo gufashwa gupfa.

Bas agira ati: " Mama yari yarafashe icyemezo ntakuka, nta gushidikanya. Ariko papa we byasaga nkaho byaramukoze ku mutima cyane

Jan yabajije umuhungu we niba koko bari gukora igikwiriye. Ibyo byatangaje Bas, kuko yatekerezaga ko nyina ari we wari gushidikanya ku cyemezo bari bafashe.

Bas agira ati: "Mama yaryohewe n' ubuzima cyane. Ndibuka ko yigeze kumbwira ati: 'Nifuza cyane kuzarama nkageza ku myaka 80, cyangwa wenda no kuri 90.'"

Ariko se yari amaze imyaka isaga icumi avuga ku bijyanye no gufashwa gupfa, bitewe n'ububabare yari amaranye imyaka myinshi.

Bari mu modoka, Bas yahumurije se. Jan amaze gutuza, bakomeje urugendo batavugana. Bumvaga umuziki, bareba ahantu heza banyuragamo.

Mu mezi yabanje uru rugendo rw'umuryango, Bas yari yaragerageje kumvisha ababyeyi be gusubika urupfu rwabo.

Agira ati: "Nagerageje kubumvisha ko bakomeza kubaho ikindi gihe kirekireho gato. Narababazaga nti: 'Kuki tutategereza kugeza mu gihe cy'itumba, cyangwa se umwaka utaha?'"

Bas yari mu gihirahiro cy'amarangamutima. Nubwo yatekerezaga ko icyemezo cy'ababyeyi be cyo gusaba gufashwa gupfa cyari gikwiye, ntiyifuzaga ko bagenda.

Agira ati: "Data yari amaze imyaka iri hagati ya 10 na 15 muri ubwo buzima bwo kubabara, bityo, ashobora kuba yari gushobora gukomeza kwihangana indi myaka mike. Ariko ntekereza ko iyo baza gutegereza undi mwaka, mama yari guhura n'ibibazo bikomeye..."

Iyo Els aza gusubika gusaba gufashwa gupfa, yashoboraga kurushaho kuremba kubera indwara ya Alzheimer (indwara itera kwibagirwa no kwangirika k'ubwonko). Ibyo byashoboraga gutuma abaganga basanga atagifite ubushobozi bwo gufata icyemezo cyo kurangiza ubuzima bwe ku bushake bwe.

Agira ati: "Data yasezeye imodoka yanjye - yakundaga imodoka yanjye, maze aravuga ati: 'Wakoze neza', hanyuma ati: 'Urakoze'."

Bas akomeza agira ati: "Hanyuma turagenda turinjira. Tekereza gukora ikintu nk'icyo! Tekereza kuba mu mwanya wabo, gukora urwo rugendo no gutera izo ntambwe ugana aho ugiye gupfira. Ni ikintu umuntu atapfa kwemera ko kibaho."

Mu masaha abiri yakurikiyeho, abagize umuryango n'inshuti zabo barazaga bakagenda. Basubiragamo byiza bari baranyuzemo, kandi bakumva umuziki. Hari igihe kimwe Bas yatekereje gusaba guhagarika ibyo bikorwa.

Yagize ati: "Hari igihe numvaga navuga nti 'Reka tugende... Twinjire mu modoka tugende.' Ariko sinifuzaga kuvuga ikintu na kimwe cyatuma bumva badatekanye cyangwa bagatangira gushidikanya ku cyemezo bari bafashe, kuko nari narabashyigikiye muri gahunda yose gufashwa gupfa.

"Byari byiza ko bose bakomeza gutuza, maze tugakoresha uwo mwanya mu gusezeranaho."

Mbere gato ya saa yine n'igice za mu gitondo (10:30), abaganga baraje kugira ngo batere Jan na Els inshinge z'imiti yari gutuma bapfa. Bombi bari baryamye ku bitanda byo kwa muganga byegeranye. Muri ibyo bihe bya nyuma, mbere y'uko batakaza ubwenge, Bas yabonye urukundo n'ubusabane bukomeye byari bikomeje guhuza ababyeyi be.

Ati: "Mu buzima bwanjye bwose, nabonye wenda inshuro eshatu cyangwa enye gusa ababyeyi banjye bafatanye ibiganza bagendana. Ariko icyo gihe bari baryamye bafatanye ibiganza. Agira ati: "Ibyo byatumye ngira ibyishimo, kuko byanyeretse ko bari babikoze bari kumwe koko."

Bas asobanura ko igice cya mbere cy'isaha nyuma y'uko ababyeyi be bahagaritse guhumeka, cyamubereye "ukuri kw'ibyabaye", kuko ntibari bakiri bazima.

"Nyuma ni bwo umenya ukuri kw'ibibaye n'icyo bisobanuye koko – ni ibyiyumvo umuntu adashobora kwiyumvisha mbere y'uko abinyuramo."

Mu ibyo bitaro, agahinda karenze Bas. Yatangiye kugira irungu rikomeye cyane.

Agira ati: "Umubabaro utewe n'urupfu ni ikintu gikomeye cyane kunyuramo, kandi nta bavandimwe mfite, nta bakuru cyangwa bashiki banjye. Numvise ndi jyenyine rwose."

Iyo twakuze turerwa n'ababyeyi bombi, iyo umwe muri bo apfuye, dushobora gusangira n'undi ibyo mwabanyemo ndetse n'agahinda mufite, bikamufasha kwihanganira kubura uwo yakundaga. Ariko kuri Bas ho byari bitandukanye, kuko Jan na Els bombi bari bamaze gupfa

Bas aribuka ati: "Byari bimeze nk'aho amaguru yanjye yombi bayakatse."

Agahinda ke ntikari mu mutima gusa, ahubwo kagaragaraga no ku mubiri. Yamaze ibyumweru bine cyangwa bitanu yumva arwaye kandi umubiri wose umubabaza.

Agira ati: "Sinagira abandi inama yo kunyura muri ibi, kandi wenda icyo ni umwanzuro ukomeye gufata. Birashoboka ko kuri bo [ababyeyi banjye] ari cyo cyari igisubizo cyiza kurusha ibindi, ariko kubatakaza bombi icyarimwe byangizeho ingaruka zikomeye cyane."

Mu bantu bo mu Buholandi baba bateganya gusaba gufashwa gupfa, cyane cyane abafite indwara yo kwibagirwa nka Els, guhitamo igihe nyacyo cyo kurangiza ubuzima bishobora kuba ibintu bigoye cyane.

Uretse kugaragaza ko bababara mu buryo bukabije kandi butihanganirwa, abaganga bagomba no gusuzuma niba bagifite ubushobozi bwo kwifatira icyemezo cyo gupfa ku bushake bwabo.

Muganga Rozemarijn van Bruchem, inzobere mu kuvura abageze mu zabukuru akaba n'umuhanga mu myitwarire iboneye mu buvuzi (ethics), ukorera mu Kigo cy'Ubuvuzi cya Erasmus i Rotterdam, asobanura ko ibi bishobora guteza agahinda gakomeye abarwayi bafite indwara yo kwibagirwa batekereza ku gufashwa gupfa.

Agira ati: "Batekereza bati: 'Ubu ndacyabasha gufata icyo cyemezo, ariko birashoboka ko ari kare cyane. Ariko se wenda mu kwezi gutaha bizaba byarenze igihe. None se nzamenya nte igihe ngomba gutangirira ubu buryo bwo gusuzumwa kugira ngo barebe niba nujuje ibisabwa, kandi niba nshobora gufashwa gupfa? Nintinda cyane, ese sinzaba natakaje amahirwe yo kubikora?'"

Muganga van Bruchem avuga ko impamvu abarwayi be bagira iyi mpungenge ari uko gufashwa gupfa byemewe n'amategeko mu Buholandi.

Baba bazi ko kwemererwa gufashwa gupfa ku bantu bageze mu rwego rukomeye rw'indwara yo kwibagirwa bidakunze kubaho. Mu bihugu aho gufashwa gupfa bibujijwe n'amategeko, nk'u Bwongereza, abantu bafite indwara yo kwibagirwa bashobora guhura n'ibibazo byinshi, ariko ntibakunze guhura n'ikibazo cyo guhitamo hagati y'ibi byemezo bibiri bifitanye isano n'ubuzima n'urupfu, nk'uko Els yabigenje.

Mu mwaka wa 2024, Els yabwiye BBC ko we n'umugabo we batashoboraga gutegereza, kuko hari amahirwe y'uko indwara ye ya Alzheimer yari kurushaho gukomera. Jan na we yari yariyemeje gupfana na Els.

Yabwiye BBC ko bishoboka ko yari agiye gupfa mbere y'igihe, ariko ko yari amaze kubaho ubuzima bwe. Yumvaga ko ubuzima bwe bwari bwarangiye kandi ko yari yarasohoje urugendo rwe rwo ku isi.

Jan na Els bari bazi neza ko ibyemezo bafashe ku bijyanye n'uko bashakaga kurangiza ubuzima bwabo byari gushyira umutwaro ukomeye ku muhungu wabo.

Bas yitabiriye inama zose ababyeyi be bagiranaga n'abaganga babo batandukanye mu gihe cy'ibikorwa byo gusaba gufashwa gupfa. Byabaga ari ibiganiro byeruye ku muryango. Akenshi, iyo umuntu twakundaga apfuye, dusigarana ibintu twicuza, cyane cyane ibijyanye n'ibyo tutabashije kumubwira akiriho. Ariko kuri Bas si ko byagenze. Hasigaye iminsi ibiri ngo Jan na Els bagere ku munsi bari barateganyije kujya muri icyo kigo, ku wa mbere tariki ya 3 z'ukwa 6, Bas yabandikiye ibaruwa.

Avuga ati: "Iyo baruwa yari ifite amapaji agera ku munani. Ku wa gatandatu nijoro, nagiye aho bari bari mu modoka yabo yo guturamo, bwije cyane. Maze mbasomera ibaruwa yose. Yavugaga ku buzima bwacu, mbashimira ibyo bari barankoreye byose."

Jan na Els bakozwe ku mutima cyane n'iyo baruwa. Nk'uko batari abantu bakunze kugaragarizanya urukundo mu ruhame, ni na ko batari basanzwe bagaragariza umuhungu wabo urukundo mu buryo bweruye.

Bas avuga ati: "Uba wumva ko bagukunda, ariko bakabigaragaza binyuze mu byo bagukorera, aho kubikubwira mu magambo cyangwa ngo baguhobere." Akomeza agira ati: "Mama wanjye yarabikoze (mu kumpobera) kenshi nyuma y'uko afashwe n'indwara yo kwibagirwa, ariko papa we ntiyigeze abikora. Sinari narigeze mpoberwa na rimwe."

Ariko ibyo byarahindutse muri iryo joro rya nyuma ryo ku wa gatandatu, bari mu modoka yabo yo guturamo. Jan yahobeye Bas.

Agira ati: "Yabikoze nyuma yiyo baruwa. Birashoboka ko cyari kimwe mu bihe byiza cyane nagize mu buzima bwanjye.

Investment in peace while upholding international law and a rules-based international system could make La Francophonie bloc a better place to live in, UN secretary General Antonio Gutteres said on Sunday.

“As your theme reminds us, peace is our best investment,” Guterres told Francophonie leaders in a video message.

This was Gutteres’ final address to the organization as secretary-general before leaving office.

The UN secretary General Guterres warned that global military spending is now 13 times greater than development aid.

“The world is arming itself at great cost while rationing peace,” he said, adding that too many countries are being forced to choose between repaying their debts and serving their populations.

“Reinvesting in peace means supporting diplomacy, upholding international law, and sharing prosperity.”

Guterres advocates for including women and young people in decision-making processes and strengthening multilateralism.

“That starts with permanent seats for Africa on the Security Council and a fair international financial system,” he said.

“I address you for the last time as Secretary-General of the United Nations. You have been a valuable partner in the pursuit of peace, sustainable development, human rights, and multilingualism,” he said.

A match involving a team playing for the first time since the death of one of their players was abandoned because of a serious injury.

Steve Evans has criticised the performances of his Bristol Rovers players

Steve Evans insists he will leave Bristol Rovers if he is not wanted following an eighth defeat in 10 league games, but says their poor form is down to his "inconsistent" players.

A 2-0 loss to Chesterfield on Saturday leaves the Gas just four points above the relegation places, with manager Evans lambasting a first-half performance that saw him make a double substitution before the interval.

The Scot was blunt in his message to supporters after the final whistle, saying he is not one to hang about for a payoff, but called on his players to take responsibility for their performances.

"My message has always been the same," he told BBC Radio Bristol. "If I'm not wanted, I'll leave. I'm not like the others that hang on for paydays.

Spireites extend Bristol Rovers' poor league run

"Let's not mince my words. I sat on the bench for 10 seconds to have a conversation with Paul Raynor [assistant head coach], and somebody shouted when I came out, 'He's come out from hiding'.

"I answer them. I don't hide. I'm out the trenches. I don't hide. I'm not like the others hiding behind the ownership. I don't do that. I'm not doing my job, neither's Paul, neither's Byron [Anthony], neither's Tomo [Lee Tomlin].

"We're not doing our jobs, but we're being let down by inconsistent players. Poor players, in my opinion."

The 64-year-old says he will now reflect on the job he is doing at the Memorial Stadium as he looks to reverse Rovers' stuttering form but wants to see his players perform the basics week to week.

"I'll go away and think about everything," he said. "I'll go away and think about my job, am I doing my job effectively?

"Can I affect the players differently to how we're affecting them at the minute because it's certainly not right, we've got players who turn up one week and disappear for two weeks. You wouldn't recognise some of them. Paul said coming off the pitch, we have to reflect on whether we are doing our jobs.

"Passion, fight, energy, commitment – those are the basics. We delivered none of the basics in the first 30 minutes of the game and that's just simple."

Steve Evans has called on his Bristol Rovers players to do the basics

Rovers now face a tricky away trip at neighbours Cheltenham next week and Evans says he will pick a team hungry for three points.

"It's always going to be tough," he added. "You're going to Steve Cotterill's Cheltenham side, who are very good, particularly at Whaddon Road. We have to pick a team first and foremost that works hard and fights.

"I'll still turn up at 6.30 in the morning. I'll still leave at 6 o'clock at night. I still go and watch the opposition, do the analysis. What's changed? I know what's changed – inconsistent players."

MN202611_1gvldefdat1.t:
Billy Vigar died from a "significant brain injury" in September 2025

The Premier League, English Football League and Women's Super League are reviewing pitch perimeters across their clubs in light of the death of former Arsenal academy player Billy Vigar last year.

Vigar died at the age of 21 from a "significant brain injury", five days after colliding with a concrete wall surrounding a pitch while playing for non-league side Chichester City.

On the eve of this season the Football Association banned clubs from having concrete, breeze block or solid brick walls surrounding their pitches, but this only applied to the National League and Women's National League.

Now it has emerged there is work under way at the highest levels.

It is understood the Premier League carried out a survey of clubs on pitch perimeters, including on the material used and the run-off distance, in light of Vigar's death.

The top flight also shared the outcome of the FA's review with clubs.

BBC Sport has approached the Premier League for comment on the outcome of its pitch survey.

The EFL also issued a survey to clubs at the start of this year to build a picture of the perimeter structure at each ground.

This also sought information about run-off distances, surfaces and gradients, and any other trip hazards.

BBC Sport understands specific health and safety assessments have been recommended for clubs found to have high-risk perimeters, in order to mitigate risk.

This survey was in addition to the regular work carried out at the beginning of the 2025-26 season, and came as a result of Vigar's death.

Meanwhile, in the WSL and WSL2 there is an acknowledgement that many of the grounds are shared with men's teams in other leagues.

The police investigation into Vigar's death is ongoing, with a further hearing scheduled for 10 February.

The Metropolitan Police expects there will be another "two to three months" before any conclusion is reached.

Vigar's parents, Keith and Camilla, told BBC Sport on the one-year anniversary that "the FA could have stopped Billy losing his life because they had so many warnings".

BBC Sport is investigating incidents involving pitch perimeters at all levels of football in England and Wales. If you have been affected by any such incident, please contact us.

MN202611_pxx6pwq36q.t:
Iran and the US are vying for control of the Strait of Hormuz

Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.

The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.

Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".

It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.

The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.

Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.

As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.

Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."

In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."

Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.

The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.

Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube channel of his lawyer

A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.

The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.

Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.

"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.

He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.

"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.

The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.

The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".

Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.

The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

Can smart glasses exam cheating be stopped?

A series of cases involving exam cheating with AI glasses in South Korea has universities and schools scrambling to rein in the use of the technology.

Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.

Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.

"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.

It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.

Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.

Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.

Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

Exams watchdog warns of rise in high-tech cheating

MN202611_137zylbsv25.t:
The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment

Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

MN202611_1xu597zxdhp.t:
Rwanda and Cambodia have launched a pilot initiative to connect their digital payment systems, paving the way for faster, more convenient and potentially cheaper cross-border money transfers between the two countries.

The initiative, known as the Proof of Concept of Cross-Border Remittance between the Kingdom of Cambodia and the Republic of Rwanda, was officially launched on November 15, 2026, on the sidelines of the Black Swan Summit Cambodia in Phnom Penh.

The project brings together Cambodia’s Bakong payment platform and Rwanda’s eKash digital payment system, operated by R-Switch, to enable people in Cambodia to send money directly to beneficiaries in Rwanda.

Under the arrangement, recipients in Rwanda will be able to receive funds through their bank accounts or mobile phones, offering an additional channel for international money transfers.

ACLEDA Bank Plc. of Cambodia will serve as the correspondent bank, while I&M Bank (Rwanda) Plc. will handle the receipt and processing of funds to ensure they reach the intended beneficiaries.

Through the partnership, customers of ACLEDA Bank and other financial institutions connected to the Bakong network will be able to transfer money directly to bank accounts and other eligible beneficiaries in Rwanda.

The initiative is expected to reduce the time and procedural requirements involved in cross-border transfers while making the services more affordable and accessible to users.

Beyond personal remittances, the integration is also expected to support trade, investment and tourism by simplifying financial transactions between individuals and businesses operating in the two countries.

Businesses engaged in cross-border activities could benefit from more convenient payment options, while improved access to digital financial services is expected to encourage greater participation in formal financial systems.

The initiative comes as Rwanda and Cambodia continue to explore opportunities to strengthen bilateral cooperation in several areas, including investment, tourism, air transport and technology.

By connecting their digital payment infrastructure, the two countries are seeking to facilitate financial transactions and create new opportunities for economic engagement between their respective markets.

MN202611_15jbf4nhohh.t:
Unconfirmed reports indicate that the new Secretary General for the La Francophonie organisation is already a concluded matter.

Taarifa Investigative Desk has learned in emerging reports from those close to the nucleus of the organization that Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo has been reelected.

From consistent diplomatic sources, Mushikiwabo reportedly received 26 votes out of 51 cast this Monday morning in Phnom Penh, during the closed-door meeting of OIF heads of state.

For a period of one hour and 22 minutes of closed-door deliberations, the 53 heads of state and government of the full members of the OIF cast their vote to select the next secretary-general for 2027–2030.

The final tally shows 51 votes cast and 2 absent: Mushikiwabo (Rwanda): 26 votes, Coumba Bâ (Mauritania): 18 votes, and Dacian Cioloș (Romania): 7 votes.

Under the 2022 rules at OIF, Mushikiwabo secures third term by a simple majority. This becomes the first vote to fully apply the 2022 reforms.

The source said that the official announcement could be made at 10:15 a.m local time by the Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet.

“let’s wait for the announcement” Rwanda’s Foreign Affairs Minister Oliveir Nduhungirehe said while leaving closed-door meeting with a broad smile.

The Mauritanian camp said,“If the result is confirmed, Mauritania will congratulate the winner. We put forward a candidacy for unity.”

Kinshasa delegation could not hold their impatience. At 9:35 a.m., they left the convention center without waiting for the official announcement.

France’s media giant Le Monde interviewed an adviser to the DRC presidency and said, “With 26 votes out of 53 members, Mushikiwabo does not have the legitimacy.”

The advisor added, “In accordance with what was announced, the DRC is suspending its participation in OIF bodies as of today.”

MN202611_gd8l0x1hhr.t:
Watch: Pat McFadden refuses to rule out that some young people might lose benefits

The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.

Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague".

McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed.

But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers.

It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work.

His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade.

However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year.

Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job.

He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness.

How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted.

Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service.

Watch: Helen Whately says legal guarantee of work or training for under-25s 'doesn't make sense'

Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this."

He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to."

He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today".

Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added.

Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending.

But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs".

She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing.

Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said:

a sustainable reduction in welfare spending cannot be achieved in two or three years, warning that "crude cuts" to the benefits system would create other additional costs for government

GPs should not be responsible for signing sick notes declaring people unable to work

ministers should "look very carefully" at Labour's manifesto commitment to phase out the reduced minimum wage for those aged 18-21, adding that moves towards this had "imposed a lot of cost" on firms

It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage.

From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently.

It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year .

French language is steadily growing it’s influence and is currently the world’s fourth most spoken language.

The French language comes behind English, Mandarin Chinese and Spanish as one of the world’s most used languages, according to the International Organisation of Francophonie (OIF).

Currently there are 396 million French speakers worldwide in 2025 compared to standard Arabic’s 335 million.

OIF figures indicate that African continent hosts 65% of French speakers.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo has the largest number, with just over 57 million French speakers, followed by Algeria with more than 15 million and Morocco with nearly 14 million.

Louis Mushikiwabo the secretary General of the OIF said in her report that there will be 590 million people speaking French by 2050.

Only around 90 million have French as their mother tongue.

“Nine out of ten of whom will live in Africa”, said Mushikiwabo,

She predicted the future of French “will no longer be shaped in Paris, but rather in Abidjan, Beirut, Brussels, Dakar, Kinshasa, Montreal, Port-au-Prince, Tunis or Yaoundé”.

French is the second most widely studied foreign language in the world – after English – with nearly 170 million learners worldwide.

While French remains a key language in diplomacy, tourism and international law.

MN202611_hw9yln1w09.t:
Alan Ruschel signed for Juventude in 2023

Alan Ruschel, a survivor of the 2016 plane crash that was carrying the Chapecoense football team, won promotion to Brazil's Serie A in his final game before retirement.

Ruschel, 37, was one of just six survivors when the plane crashed in Colombia and killed 71 people, including 19 of the club's players and the coaching staff.

Despite severe injuries and spinal surgery, Ruschel returned to football a year later and retires after earning promotion to Brazil's top flight with Juventude, his boyhood club which he re-joined in 2023.

Ruschel came off the bench in the 74th minute to help see out a 2-0 win over Botafogo, resulting in an emotional farewell with a lap of honour at the club's Alfredo Jaconi Stadium.

Before the game, he was also carried into the stadium on the shoulders of fans.

"I arrived here in 2007 with the club in Serie A and I am leaving the club there as well," Ruschel told a Brazilian television station after the match.

"My body wasn't responding any more. I had two consecutive knee surgeries, so I was starting to fighting with my own body.

"It wasn't working any more, even though being on the pitch was always a pleasure."

Ruschel referenced the plane crash in a video on social media which he posted the day before the game to confirm his retirement.

"Football has given me wonderful moments, but life has put me in front of challenges that I never imagined. November 29, 2016, a day that changed my life forever.

"I lost friends, companions and people with whom I shared dreams and projects.

"And God gave me a second chance. I didn't know if I would be able to play football again, but I believed that if I was here, there was still a purpose for my life.

"And today, I have the privilege of being able to choose the moment to say goodbye."

Tenefire fans display a banner paying tribute to Jesus de Miguel

Tenerife played their first game since the death of striker Jesus de Miguel on an emotional day at the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez stadium.

De Miguel died at the age of 30 on 3 November, a day after colliding with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a home match in Spain's Segunda Division.

Tenerife beat bottom side Ceuta 2-0 on Sunday, with tributes to De Miguel paid both before and during the game.

Lengthy standing ovations preceded and followed a minute of silence before the match.

In the ninth minute play was stopped and a round of applause took place, while a video of De Miguel was shown in the stadium, as happened at all first- and second-tier games in Spain last weekend.

Tenerife fans displayed a banner that read: "Jesus de Miguel, 9, eternally blue and white."

Forward Nacho Gil opened the scoring for the home side in the 40th minute and celebrated by holding up De Miguel's shirt.

Gil revealed a message written under his shirt that read: "Demi, always in our hearts."

Neal Viereck scored four minutes from time as Tenerife ended a run of six games without a win. They are 14th in the table.

Tenerife's game with Granada on 7 November was postponed and the club invited fans to the stadium to pay their respects to De Miguel.

Owono was given a 12-match suspension by the Spanish football federation for the challenge which resulted in De Miguel's death.

The federation has ruled that the game between Tenerife and Andorra, which was abandoned seven minutes into stoppage time after the incident occurred, will not be replayed and the 2-2 score will stand.

Czech radio said it's the largest protest in the history of the independent Czech Republic

Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the license fee and use the state budget to fund public media.

Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom.

The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.

Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests.

Czech households currently pay ⁠205 crowns ($9.44, £7.06) a month for Czech TV and Czech radio.

Organisers say the protest in Prague's Letna park has "roughly 400,000" attendees, making it the largest protest since the country's independence in 1993

Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended.

It is being described as the largest protest since the Czech Republic's independence in 1993.

"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency.

"If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."

Some protesters wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as a tribute to an animated character, Večerníček, who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children's bedtime stories for decades.

Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who tightly controlled state media when he was in power.

Prime Minister Andrej Babis was appointed in December in 2025, and has faced criticism over his coalition's attacks on Czech media.

"Political attacks against private and public media have become one of the hallmarks of Andrej Babis' premiership," said Pavol Szalai, Prague Bureau director of international press freedom organisation Reporters Without Borders, in June.
