MN202611_1yyes7csqp2.t:
Africa CDC Director-General Dr Jean Kaseya speaks at an earlier event

ADDIS ABABA – Rwanda and Uganda offer important lessons in preparing for and responding to public health emergencies, Africa CDC Director General Dr Jean Kaseya has said.

In the meantime, the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to battle an Ebola outbreak six months after its declaration.

Speaking during a virtual media briefing to mark six months since the outbreak was declared in the DRC, Kaseya called for stronger government leadership, greater community involvement and closer cooperation between African countries to contain the disease.

He said governments must take ownership of outbreak responses by investing in preparedness, training health workers and strengthening public health systems.

International partners, he added, should coordinate their support under national government leadership.

Kaseya cited Rwanda and Uganda as examples of the importance of preparedness and organised national responses in managing public health threats.

He said controlling an outbreak requires more than medical supplies and treatment facilities. It also depends on strong institutions, public confidence and coordination across all levels of society.

The briefing came as the regional Ebola response recorded different developments across affected countries.

Kenya and Nigeria have entered the 42-day countdown towards declaring their respective Ebola outbreaks over. The period is a critical stage in the process, requiring continued surveillance and vigilance before health authorities can officially declare an outbreak ended.

The developments offer grounds for cautious optimism.

However, Kaseya warned against shifting attention away from the DRC, where the outbreak remains a major concern.

He stressed that the response in the country is far from over and called for sustained efforts to prevent further transmission.

A major focus of the briefing was the role of communities in controlling Ebola.

Kaseya advocated a village-centred approach that places local leaders and residents at the heart of the response. He said public health interventions must reflect local realities and address the concerns of the people most affected.

Building trust is essential, he said. Communities must understand why health authorities introduce particular measures and what they can do to protect themselves and others.

He argued that residents should not be treated merely as recipients of public health instructions. They are important partners in identifying risks, raising concerns and preventing further transmission.

Regional cooperation was another key issue.

Kaseya called for stronger cross-border surveillance, faster detection of suspected cases and better coordination between neighbouring countries.

With people constantly moving across national borders, he said, no country can treat epidemic preparedness as an isolated national responsibility. Timely information-sharing and coordinated action are essential to limiting the spread of infectious diseases.

The briefing also highlighted the role of journalists in public health emergencies.

Kaseya urged media organisations to provide accurate and timely information, challenge misinformation and help communities understand how to protect themselves.

Rumours and inaccurate reporting can undermine public confidence and weaken the response, particularly during health emergencies.

Journalists, he said, can help bridge the gap between health authorities and communities by translating technical information into accessible reporting while ensuring that public concerns reach decision-makers.

Marking six months since the DRC outbreak was declared, Kaseya thanked Africa CDC’s media partners for their continued engagement. He encouraged them to maintain regular communication with the continental health agency.

His central message was that controlling Ebola requires more than an emergency response. It calls for sustained political leadership, prepared health systems, trusted community partnerships and cooperation across national borders.

The continuing situation in the DRC, alongside the experiences of Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria, underscores the importance of preparedness and public trust in protecting populations against infectious disease threats.

MN202611_1xl6gth5uj.t:
A draw in Hungary on Tuesday would secure promotion to Nations League A for Northern Ireland

Still the only side in the 2026-27 Nations League yet to concede a goal, Northern Ireland know that one more clean sheet will be enough to secure back-to-back promotions.

After Saturday's 1-0 victory over Ukraine in Belfast, a draw away to Hungary in Budapest on Tuesday night would ensure Michael O'Neill's team top their group and advance to League A for the first time.

With three wins and two draws from their five games played, the visitors to the Puskas Arena are in the box seat in Group B2, but they will travel targeting victory rather than the draw that would suffice.

"We try and win every single game. If you don't, there's no point going," said veteran striker Josh Magennis, who will win a 94th cap should he feature.

"It's a weird [situation], but Michael's already told us that we're going to be set up to win.

"To have that in your back pocket is obviously nice, and the onus is going to be on them, but we're going to win it as much as them."

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC One NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

Northern Ireland were in a similar situation in the Nations League two years ago, albeit in the third tier, when needing a point away against Luxembourg to secure promotion.

They flew out of the blocks and raced into a 2-0 lead, only to allow a Luxembourg comeback in the second half, resulting in a nervy finish for a 2-2 draw.

Shea Charles was captain that night in November 2024 and believes the squad have taken a lesson from their loss of control in the fixture.

"I think we would have learnt from that time," said the Fulham midfielder.

"We were really comfortable in the game and let it slip a little bit.

"But we still came away with the draw and that's all that we needed. I'm really looking forward to it and I think we can go there and put in a good performance."

Charles echoed Magennis' sentiment that the permutations around the result will not alter the way the side approach the game.

He said: "I think we'll still try and go there and win. We know it's going to be a challenge, a very good team and a big crowd, I assume. It'll be tough.

"We've got to go out there and play the way we've been playing."

Sixteen years after his international debut, Magennis is the longest-serving player in O'Neill's squad and the sole survivor from Northern Ireland's only previous win in Budapest.

An unused substitute in the 2-1 victory that kicked off their successful Euro 2016 qualifying campaign, Magennis believes the squad's changing profile over the years has set them up well to target all three points.

"I've played in a lot of Northern Ireland teams where we've been very reactive to the opposition, trying to nullify them, but this is the type of group where we're able to overpower and overrun games and they'll have to think about us," he said.

Coming into this campaign, Northern Ireland's ability to grind out results beyond Windsor Park had been called into question.

Wins away to Georgia and Ukraine already in this campaign have changed that perception, and Magennis feels Hungary - one point behind Northern Ireland - will know the visitors are not to be underestimated.

"If they don't show us the respect that we deserve, then it'll be at their own peril, and they'll learn the hard way come 90 minutes when we take the three points," added the Stevenage striker.

"If they don't account for our running power, our physicality, our set-pieces, all that type of stuff, then that's down to them.

"We only play the team that's in front of us, but we'll go into it fully [prepared]."

MN202611_h94m5dwjjz.t:
Imane Touriss ended this year's Women's Champions League with four goals after her double in the final

Moroccan club AS FAR became the first team to retain the Women's African Champions League title with a hard-fought 3-1 win over Mamelodi Sundowns.

Imane Touriss put the North Africans ahead in the 23rd minute in Ismaila, Egypt, when her early shot from outside the box caught out Sundowns goalkeeper Andile Dlamini.

But the South African side levelled two minutes later through a stunning effort from Refilwe Tholakele, who flashed a right-footed shot from a narrow angle across goal and inside the right-hand post.

Seventeen-year-old right-back Hiba Youssoufi restored the lead eight minutes before half-time when her shot from 12 yards was deflected in off Sundowns defender Asanda Hadebe.

And, as the Brazilians pushed forward in search of an equaliser, an unmarked Touriss made it 3-1 with 13 minutes remaining with a low first-time finish from the middle of the area after fine work down the right flank by Fatima Tagnaout.

Ronnel Donnelly had scored a hat-trick for Sundowns in their semi-final victory over Kawempe Muslim Ladies but was largely kept quiet by the AS FAR defence.

The closest the Brazilians came to an equaliser in the second half was when substitute Nthabiseng Majiya had an effort deflected wide, and they failed to test AS FAR goalkeeper Khadija Er-Rmichi after going two goals down.

AS FAR, who had surprisingly lost their opening game at the finals to Ugandan outfit Kawempe Muslim Ladies, are the first side to win the Women's African Champions League title three times and also take home $600,000 (£449,000) in prize money.

The side representing Morocco's armed forces add to their triumph in 2022, when they beat Sundowns 4-0, and last year's victory over ASEC Mimosas of Ivory Coast.

Sundowns have claimed the title twice themselves, winning the inaugural competition in 2021 and lifting the trophy again two years later.

AS FAR players scooped the individual awards, with Touriss winning the golden boot with four goals, captain Ghizlane Chebbak named the player of the tournament and Er-Rmichi awarded the golden glove.

MN202611_1jg5s1ej3io.t:
Burundi’s Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana has attacked Rwanda’s candidature for the Secretary General of Francophonie organisation.

The next Secretary General of the 90- member strong organisation will be announced tomorrow morning before 10Am according to insiders in the OIF.

“A third term for Louise as secretary-general would bury the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF),” Bizimana claimed late Sunday.

Bizimana also denounced what he described an attempt to impose a candidacy on member states, arguing that it would serve particular interests rather than those of the organisation.

He threatened that with Mushikiwabo getting reelected, “Burundi will take note of this and will logically withdraw from the organization.”

Back home, Burundi maintains a frosty relations with Neighbouring Rwanda. Burundi shut up it’s doors since 2015 accusing it’s Northern neighbour of interference in it’s domestic matters.

Burundi has since signed a military cooperation agreement with Kinshasa. Congolese troops are deployed alongside with Burundi forces in a military campaign against the battle hardened FRN rebels they jointly accuse of receiving support from Kigali.

The FRN rebels currently control large parts of North and South Kivu provinces.

Rwanda told the la Francophonie that it will not withdraw Louis Mushikiwabo’s candidature.

Insiders with close understanding of the matter behind closed doors in Phnom Penh claimed that French leader Emmanuel Macron urged Rwanda to withdraw Mushikiwabo’s candidacy,

“Attempts by Kinshasa and Paris to blackmail Rwanda ultimately undermine a fair election to block Louise Mushikiwabo’s re-election,” a social commentator noted.

Political pundits argue that the DRC-Rwanda contest in Cambodia may attract attention to the 2025 precedent.

Rwanda effectively pulled out of the Economic Community of Central African States (ECCAS) after DRC-led opposition blocked its expected rotating presidency.

“Kigali may again choose institutional exit over political subordination,” a social commentator said.

An African Intelligence source claims the President Felix Tshisekedi of DRC has instructed the information Minister Patrick Muyaya to prepare a letter announcing the DRC’s withdrawal from the organisation should Mushikiwabo be declared winner.

The letter is said to have been presented to several African ministers present in Phnom Penh to make it clear to them that the DRC’s threat of withdrawal is not merely a statement of intent.

MN202611_1ewru40kqku.t:
The singer-songwriter bought the former home of fashion designer Laura Ashley in 2021

Charlotte Church will close her wellness retreat after five "beautiful years", the company has announced.

The Dreaming, based in Rhydoldog House near Rhayader, Powys, offered retreats aimed at helping people reconnect with nature and spirituality.

The singer-songwriter bought the former home of fashion designer Laura Ashley in 2021, with its renovation later featuring in a Discovery Channel documentary series.

Last month, the team at the retreat announced it would be "pausing" operations to "reassess" what it should offer.

But it has now confirmed it is shutting down.

In a statement on social media, the team said they had hoped it would be a "period of hibernation, rather than an ending," but have come to realise it is the "end of our journey with The Dreaming".

"What a beautiful, wild and wonderful few years it has been," the post added.

"We've shared stories, made friendships, held space for one another and found moments of stillness in a world that so rarely allows us to slow down.

"Thousands of you have found your way to this little corner of the Welsh hills, each bringing something of yourselves, and each leaving a little something behind. You have made The Dreaming what it is."

Last month the business said it was in the process of "germinating new dreams for the future" and was set to "hibernate".

Rhydoldog House was the former proerty of fashion designer Laura Ashley

Earlier this year, Church said that The Dreaming was a response to the pressures of contemporary life.

She said: "I am really passionate about what we do, because I believe more than ever the world and the people of the world are in dire need of being held through some very difficult times.

"There are some very difficult transitional times for us as human beings on this Earth.

"This is also due to the excesses in which society is so much based around, capitalist values and ideologies, meaning there is then less around care, people, community, nature and belonging. We are crying out for these things, every single one of us."

Church previously confessed she had blown "pretty much all my life savings" on the £1.5m, seven-bedroom property.

The house, with origins in the 15th Century, belonged to textile, fashion and retail entrepreneur Ashley and her husband Bernard and was owned by the family until his death in 2009.

A planning application for the retreat in 2021 said Church wanted to transform Rhydoldog House into a carbon neutral wellbeing and healing retreat with four log cabins in the grounds as tourist accommodation.

Since opening, The Dreaming hosted more than 3,000 guests and offered a "pay what you can" scheme starting at £1 per night, as well as free stays for NHS workers.

Restrictions have affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones

A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.

The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.

Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said.

US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says

Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.

The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.

Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".

It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.

The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.

On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting Ukrainian electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".

"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.

Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.

Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.

It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.

Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.

Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.

Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.

Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.

"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.

"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."

Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.

In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.

Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.

Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.

The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.

"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

MN202611_69xf9vtenl.t:
Ronaldinho played the first 45 minutes for Ravenna against Forli

Brazil legend Ronaldinho made his comeback aged 46 for Ravenna in their Italian third-tier derby against Forli.

The 46-year-old came out of retirement for the Serie C club he joined as an investor in August, having last played in 2015 for Fluminense.

He started Sunday's game and showed some bright touches, and he was involved in the opening goal.

The former Barcelona superstar held off a defender before playing the pass that came before the assist for Giulio Donati's drive from outside the box.

He had earlier set up a chance for Donati from a corner, with the defender having his header saved.

At half-time there was a media circus around Ronaldinho, with journalists surrounding him, and former Brazil and AC Milan team-mate Dida joined him on the pitch.

Ronaldinho was substituted at the break.

A temporary stand, named the R10 in reference to Ronaldinho and his familiar shirt number, was built for the sold-out fixture at the Stadio Bruno Benelli.

The game was streamed in several countries around the world.

Ronaldinho trained once with the team, on Saturday, before Sunday's debut.

A team graphic beforehand showed him on the left side, but he mostly played centrally.

In his peak playing years, Ronaldinho was one of the best players in the world - as well as one of the most popular for his joyful demeanour and exuberant skill.

He won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil, the 2006 Champions League with Barcelona, and league titles with Barca and AC Milan - plus the Ballon d'Or and Fifa World Player of the Year awards in 2005.

He also played for Paris St-Germain as well as Gremio, Flamengo, Atletico Mineiro and Fluminense in his homeland, plus Mexican side Queretaro.

Ronaldinho scored 299 goals in his regular career and had been hoping to have a chance for number 300 for Ravenna. He would have taken a penalty had they been awarded one.

It is not clear if he plans to play again for Ravenna, who are second in their Serie C group.

MN202611_13igfi08cwm.t:
Sebastien Pocognoli worked with Louis van Gaal at AZ Alkmaar

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli says he draws on the influence of iconic manager Louis van Gaal in his own coaching career.

The Belgian worked under the legendary Dutchman during their time at AZ Alkmaar, a special period for Pocognoli during which he won the Eredivisie title in 2009.

Van Gaal also previously took charge of the Netherlands, and now that he has moved into international football himself, the Scotland boss reflected on the 75-year-old's influence.

"I take a lot from all of my gaffers, but probably he was the one with the most experience," Pocognoli told BBC Scotland.

"I was very young and you know in that moment he had all the Barcelona young players between his hands, also Ajax players.

"The way that he treats the young players in a direct way, honest way and hard way was for me really inspiring in my daily job now.

"I was lucky to have a lot of good coaches but he was probably the most that impressed me day by day, and I felt progress under him.

"That I think is the best thing for players as a feeling."

Progress is exactly what every Scotland fan is yearning for. Under Steve Clarke, the amount of that very commodity plateaued.

Years in the international wilderness were expelled with two European Championships and a World Cup appearance, but they were punctuated by disappointing results and dour tactics.

Pocognoli's arrival signified not only a new era, but a new approach, formation, selection and outlook.

It has been far from straightforward for the Belgian as he approaches 100 days in charge next week. Five games, two wins over North Macedonia, a draw in Slovenia and two humbling defeats mark his tenure so far.

Within it, a fresh system and injection of different faces to offer a break from the norm, but also plenty signs that a transformation will not be an immediate reality.

Scotland's failings in front of goal has remained, while it is clear the Scots are still getting to grips with a back three, albeit with enforced changes in personnel.

"Everything in life takes time to build if you want to achieve something," said Pocognoli.

Scotland to play with bravery and courage - Pocognoli

You are Scotland boss Pocognoli - what would you do?

Six goals to go - will McGinn catch Dalglish & Law?

"So we know that in the performance world everything goes faster and quicker, but we have an objective and we know that we have to go through the up and down and the good moments. At the end I hope that all this experience can make us stronger.

"I don't ask the players to be patient, it's just to believe in what we are doing."

Pocognoli acknowledges he's not had much opportunity to immerse himself in Scottish culture after taking his first foray into international management.

A wander around Glasgow is about all he's managed. And any further exploring will have to wait until after Monday's Nations League test in St Gallen.

Finishing in the top two of their group seems a tall order for Scotland, who are requiring a win and snookers in Slovenia. It seems progression to the next Euros will instead roll on to the qualifying campaign next year.

"We don't have the control of what will happen because Slovenia will decide," Pocognoli said. "But if we want to have a chance to go through to the group stage and to go to the play-offs we have to go with the bravery and try to play with courage and try to force something.

"I don't believe that we are waiting for something then it will happen, so let's go through our quality and try to be aggressive and wait what happens in Slovenia."

MN202611_1x5kabm8wo0.t:
Fiji boss Jake White (left) believes Andy Farrell (right) and Ireland must improve before facing South Africa

Former South Africa head coach Jake White said his Fiji side "did Ireland a favour" in Saturday's Nations Championship contest before the Irish face the Springboks in Dublin next week.

Fiji lost 43-15 to Ireland at Aviva Stadium having frustrated Andy Farrell's side during a closely contested first half.

While Ireland scored 26 unanswered points in the second half, White - who led South Africa to World Cup glory in 2007 - suggested Farrell's team cannot afford similarly sluggish spells against the back-to-back world champions, who won 24-13 in Dublin last year.

"We were playing a little bit like South Africa to be honest, I think that sums it up," said the 62-year-old.

"We were letting Ireland have the ball and we were happy to defend against them and we were happy for them to try to outwork us."

Asked to assess Ireland and South Africa's highly-anticipated meeting on Saturday (16:40 GMT), White added: "Well, I think we probably did Ireland a favour today.

"Let me put it that way, because I think Ireland deep down know that if they play like that against South Africa, they're gonna be up against it."

Ireland score seven tries in victory over Fiji in Dublin

Ireland shake off sluggish start to brush aside Fiji

White, who was appointed Fiji boss last month, was frustrated that his side opted to take a tap penalty instead of a scrum when the game was in the balance in the second half.

"I know how South Africa operate and they would've taken that scrum there, they would have backed the fact that they wanted to get [Ireland] a yellow card," said White.

"They would have taken another scrum and another scrum and another scrum, and they wouldn't have worried about the ref making a call about collapsing or early engaging.

"The five-metre line-outs that we didn't take opportunities in, and the five-metre scrum and tap penalties, South Africa will turn those into points and I'm sure that Andy [Farrell] and the players will be aware of that.

"They [Ireland] have been around a long time, and they know what's coming, and that's probably why he picked the team that he did because he wanted to make sure that they get a little bit more gun-ready for next weekend, because the easiest thing would have been to change the team and then they're probably one game shy of playing South Africa next week."

White added: "If I'm coaching South Africa and Malcolm Marx is standing there [as captain], there's no way he is going to say, 'we'll take the tap'. There's no way that happens.

"Malcolm Marx will say, 'let's take the scrum,' or 'we'll kick it out into the corner and we'll take the line-out'. And that's because they back themselves in those situations."

A short but sweet Ireland cameo for James McNabney

When White's comments were put to Farrell, the Ireland boss said: "We were just saying in the changing rooms that we learned some good lessons and we'll use them in the right manner for next week."

Farrell also admitted the scoreline flattered his side after they pulled clear having only led 17-15 at the break.

"Pleased to get the win, especially the scoreline, it flattered us a little bit but having said that you've got to work for those points and after 25 minutes you're down by five points against a side that's playing pretty well," said Farrell.

"As far as the physical nature of the game, I thought they were winning collisions, they were good in the air and on the floor, running really physically through the line and the breakdown was pretty good.

"All in all, we need to understand that wins here when you're under a bit of pressure, they're all pretty precious."

While Ireland struggled to click at times, Farrell was impressed by James McNabney's shorter-than-expected debut.

The Ulster back row came off the bench and made two huge carries before being forced off with a head injury which rules the 23-year-old out of featuring against South Africa.

"He's joking in the changing rooms - he's delighted with himself for the shortest cameo of a first cap," he said of McNabney.

"I reckon it's the best cameo of three-and-a-half minutes or whatever it was on a debut in Irish history really.

"He remembers the two breaks that he made, so he seems in good spirits."

A football tournament for nine and 10 year olds in Bergamo, Italy, was abandoned because of the behaviour of parents, which included fighting and shouting homophobic insults towards a child and a referee.

The tournament was arranged by Serie D club Villa Valle, and Italian news agency Ansa reported , external that the referees used were young people involved at the club.

Organisers of the event and the coaches of all teams involved agreed to suspend the tournament during the final match of the day because of the parents' quarrels which also included spitting and booing opposing teams.

It also said that some children left the pitch crying.

Villa Valle posted a statement on social media, condemning the behaviour which they described as "painful to witness", but also praised the attitudes of the children playing and their coaches.

"Villa Valle wishes to express its strongest condemnation of the disrespectful and violent behaviour displayed by some parents in the stands," the club said.

"With deep disappointment, our club found itself compelled to take a decision that was as difficult as it was necessary: to bring the final match of the tournament to an early end and to suspend the awards ceremony, in order to send a strong and unequivocal message against attitudes that have nothing whatsoever to do with the values of sport.

"After a day characterised by matches played in a spirit of fairness, mutual respect and sportsmanship by the young athletes and coaching staff, it was particularly painful to witness such deplorable incidents in the stands.

"We strongly believe in the educational value of sport, especially at youth level, and we are convinced that adults should serve as positive role models for young people, not become the protagonists of behaviour that risks undermining the true meaning of these events."

Izzy Goodwin scored from her one shot on target against Arsenal

After 10 games in the Women's Super League season, London City Lionesses have shown they are capable of finishing inside the top three.

Their narrow 2-1 defeat by Manchester City two weeks ago provided snippets of their potential but a 1-1 draw at the Emirates against an improved Arsenal on Sunday confirmed their credentials.

Eder Maestre's side sit third in the table - the last qualification spot for next season's Women's Champions League - and are six points above Arsenal.

It is a strong position to be in just shy of the halfway stage having already faced big hitters Arsenal, Manchester City and Manchester United.

Current leaders Chelsea await in December but, for now, London City's progress is moving at a pace that looks set to challenge the usual suspects.

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Goodwin's glorious solo strike draws London City Lionesses level

A sold-out away end helped fill out the 32,000-strong crowd at the Emirates on Sunday as many hoped for an end-to-end encounter.

They were not disappointed as fearless London City showed bravery against an Arsenal side who played with a spark following their 1-1 draw with Barcelona.

The visitors were helped out by Arsenal's wastefulness - the Gunners had 17 shots and only converted one - but London City caused plenty of problems of their own.

Maestre said after their defeat by Manchester City that their opponents showed more experience and know-how but against Arsenal, his side matured.

They were under pressure early on and fell a goal down thanks to Frida Maanum's opener but it took just 98 seconds for Izzy Goodwin to equalise for London City.

That killed Arsenal's momentum and when the pressure increased again from the hosts in the second half, goalkeeper and player of the match Mary Earps stepped up to make crucial saves.

"The performance was there. We had the chances to score and get a better result but Arsenal had chances too. The game was very open," said Maestre.

"The way we faced and challenged every circumstance in the game shows we are here, and able to play with that mentality in these big games.

"We came here to take risks. Our energy was good. We were brave and weren't scared about the context or the opponent.

"We tried to play as if we were at home. I always want to feel that my teams are brave and go for the win."

That bravery showed as Alexia Putellas came close twice with long-range efforts, Goodwin could have been onside when she was played in behind later on.

London City hit the crossbar through substitute Delphine Cascarino and had 14 shots compared to Arsenal's 17, including four inside the box.

Arsenal are still yet to win at home this season in the WSL but this was still an impressive showing from London City, who came to the Emirates to play.

But while they were willing to take risks, they were smarter than they were against Manchester City, choosing when to press aggressively and when to hold off.

"We tried to match the pace of the ball and not expose ourselves as much to the players that Arsenal have," added Maestre.

"We were trying to mix the moments we were more clinical in our press. We made some adjustments at half-time and were much better at recognising those."

Mary Earps made eight saves in the 1-1 draw with Arsenal

London City are backed by US billionaire Michele Kang and that has made a big difference in the transfer market.

They recruited superstars Alexia Putellas, Mary Earps, Mapi Leon and Kadidiatou Diani in the summer.

Such is their depth that high-flying Spaniard Lucia Corrales, the dangerous Cascarino and England international Freya Godfrey came off the bench.

Those individual talents have made a difference and on Sunday it was goalkeeper Earps who took the plaudits, claiming the player of the match award.

She made crucial saves late on as Arsenal pushed ferociously for a winner, tipping Maanum's effort onto the crossbar and blocking her shot from close range.

Earps had to bide her time for the number one shirt after making the switch from Paris St-Germain this summer but has started the past three WSL games.

"Mary is a very strong character and is much more than the things we see in terms of the performance," said Maestre.

"She has experience, and energy that you can bring to every part in the process and not just the things we see in the matches.

"I think the energy that she brings to the position is massive and has a massive impact. I'm very pleased with her."

Watching on in the stands was England boss Sarina Wiegman who will have been pleased with the display from goalscorer Goodwin.

The 23-year-old got the better of England captain Leah Williamson when she fooled her with quick feet and fired the ball into the back of the net, making it 1-1.

She is proof that competition for places in the London City starting XI is pushing players on and that their depth is improving each week.

"I think Izzy is becoming a more mature player. She has the inner competition and the signings sometimes push you to bring 100% every time," added Maestre.

"She is committed to keep pushing and, with the performances she is having, why not [earn an England call-up]?

"Izzy is moving forward in the ways she can take advantage and that commitment is the way she is reaching those performances. I'm very proud of her."

MN202611_6q2pu9vmb3.t:
'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop

Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.

"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday.

President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.

More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.

In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.

The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.

The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.

On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.

Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.

The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.

He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".

Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.

"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."

In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".

"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.

Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.

Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".

He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

MN202611_cjoip5hf5z.t:
Protesters in Dhaka, Bangladesh, on Friday demanding a new minimum wage

Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage.

Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend.

The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP.

Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis.

On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in.

A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.

Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out.

He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest".

Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close

The garment industry in Bangladesh employs about four million workers making clothes for big brands including H&M, Primark and Zara.

Bangladesh is the world's second largest exporter of ready- to-wear clothes after China and it is feared that the current unrest could have a knock-on effect for international buyers if it carries on for substantial amount of time.

The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) is calling for protection for factories.

"BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected," BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said.

"Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh's labour law."

On 1 November the government formed a minimum wage board to recommend a revised pay structure for workers.

The board, chaired by a senior district judge, said at its first meeting it would finalise any recommendations by the end of November.

Once it is put in place, the revised pay structure is expected to take effect from 1 December.

MN202611_1xq9wrhsf3v.t:
As the Francophonie prepares to choose its next secretary-general, the word “consensus” has become a diplomatic battleground.

Romanian candidate Dacian Cioloș thanked the Democratic Republic of Congo for its support, praising Kinshasa’s “trust in my vision and its commitment to consensus.”

He also thanked Juliana Amato Lumumba, the Congolese candidate, for her “commitment to the unity of the Francophonie,” adding that dialogue remained open to all.

The message presented the emerging alignment as an effort to bring members together. Rwanda’s Foreign Minister, Olivier Nduhungirehe, saw a contradiction.

In a pointed response, Nduhungirehe argued that an African country backing a non-African candidate after withdrawing its own nominee could not describe that candidate as a consensus choice “from the perspective of the African Union’s member states.”

He said the support ran against a formal African Union decision endorsing three African candidates for the post.

His argument was not that Cioloș lacked the right to run. Nduhungirehe explicitly acknowledged that the Romanian candidate remained legitimate and entitled to seek the votes of OIF member states.

His objection was to the language of consensus; a candidate might be eligible under the organisation’s rules, he argued, without representing the position African states had agreed to take.

The dispute follows Kinshasa’s withdrawal of Lumumba’s candidacy and exploring a joint approach with Romania in support of Cioloș.

The Congolese government described the move as an effort to encourage a broader consensus. As of its announcement, Lumumba’s candidacy had not been formally confirmed as withdrawn.

Now, pundits say the distinction matters. The African Union’s July decision endorsed the candidacies of Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo, the DRC’s Lumumba and Mauritania’s Coumba Bâ.

It did not name one of them as Africa’s sole candidate. The resolution called on African OIF members to choose among the three.

Nduhungirehe’s response then turned from the African Union to Europe. He said it was “rather amusing” that European countries which regularly praise democracy and electoral competition were warning at the Francophonie ministerial conference that a vote could be dangerous because it might divide the organisation.

It was a sharp charge of double standards, delivered as the OIF faces a choice between its traditional preference for consensus and a vote if members fail to agree.

The organisation’s rules allow for a simple-majority vote when consensus cannot be reached. The next secretary-general is due to be chosen in Phnom Penh on November 16.

The confrontation has exposed two competing ideas of unity. Kinshasa’s offer casts consensus as compromise between rival camps.

Kigali’s response says that compromise cannot erase a regional commitment already made, particularly when an African state is prepared to support a candidate from outside the continent.

For Cioloș, the challenge is to build support without allowing that support to be portrayed as a breach of African solidarity.

For the OIF, the question is whether unity means avoiding a contested vote or accepting one when members cannot agree.

By the time delegates gather to decide, “consensus” may no longer sound like a neutral diplomatic word. It has become the argument itself.

Romania’s most visible recent encounter with the Democratic Republic of Congo came through the barrel of a gun.

Hundreds of Romanian military contractors were deployed in eastern DRC, where they worked alongside the Congolese army in its campaign against AFC/M23.

When Goma fell in January 2025, nearly 300 of them abandoned the battlefield, sought protection at United Nations facilities and crossed into Rwanda before being flown home.

Now Romania has returned to the centre of Congolese politics through diplomacy.

The DRC has moved to withdraw its own African candidate, Juliana Amato Lumumba, and support former Romanian prime minister Dacian Cioloș for secretary-general of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie.

Cioloș presented Kinshasa’s support as an act of unity.

“My thanks to the DRC for its trust in my vision and its commitment to consensus,” he said. “Let’s move beyond competition and embrace cooperation.”

He also thanked Lumumba for her commitment to the unity of the Francophonie and declared that dialogue remained open to everyone.

Rwanda’s Foreign Minister, Olivier Nduhungirehe, responded by tearing apart the claim of consensus.

“Any non-African candidate for a position in an international organisation, backed by an African state that has withdrawn its own candidate, doing so in flagrant violation of a formal decision by the African Union, cannot logically be considered a ‘consensus candidate’ from the perspective of the African Union’s member states,” Nduhungirehe said.

His message was simple. A European candidate may be legally entitled to contest, but he cannot be presented as Africa’s consensus choice after an African government withdraws an African woman in defiance of a continental decision.

The African Union endorsed the three African women in the contest: incumbent Secretary-General Louise Mushikiwabo of Rwanda, Juliana Amato Lumumba of the DRC and Coumba Bâ of Mauritania.

Its decision called upon African members of the Francophonie to choose among them. Kinshasa instead turned to Europe.

That decision becomes even more politically uncomfortable when placed against the recent history of Romanian mercenaries in the DRC.

The Romanian contractors were part of a private military network associated with Horațiu Potra, a former member of the French Foreign Legion.

They were hired to train Congolese troops, protect strategic installations and support military operations against AFC/M23.

United Nations investigators documented the involvement of private military companies in strategic planning, reconnaissance, logistics, artillery operations and support for Congolese military aircraft. Congo Protection, which employed large numbers of Romanians, operated within this wider military structure.

But when the front collapsed, the expensive foreign force collapsed with it.

A United Nations Group of Experts report recorded that 291 Congo Protection personnel sought protection at MONUSCO facilities during the assault on Goma. Negotiations involving the United Nations and Rwanda eventually secured their evacuation to Romania through Kigali.

Images of Romanian contractors being searched, disarmed and transported through Rwanda became a humiliating symbol of Kinshasa’s failed dependence on foreign guns.

Some contractors reportedly earned thousands of dollars every month while ordinary Congolese soldiers received a fraction of that amount. Yet when Goma came under decisive pressure, the foreign fighters escaped while Congolese civilians and soldiers remained behind to face the consequences.

There is no public evidence that Cioloș was involved in recruiting, managing or deploying those mercenaries. He must therefore be judged on his own programme and political record.

But the symbolism cannot be wished away.

Romania first entered this chapter of Congo’s crisis through highly paid military contractors. After that project ended in surrender, Kinshasa is now helping a Romanian politician pursue one of the most influential diplomatic positions in the French-speaking world.

For many Africans, the sequence will look deeply troubling. The DRC hired Romanian guns, abandoned an African candidacy and then embraced a Romanian candidate under the language of “consensus.”

Consensus, however, is not created by repeating the word.

Nduhungirehe also exposed what he described as European hypocrisy. He said the same European governments that constantly lecture Africans about democracy and electoral competition were now warning that holding a vote in the Francophonie could create division.

“It is rather amusing,” he said, that European countries which praise democracy “every day” could look African delegates “straight in the eye and with their hands on their hearts” and argue that voting was dangerous.

That argument places Europe in an awkward corner.

If elections are healthy for African countries, why should an election be considered dangerous when a European candidate faces African competitors? If Cioloș has sufficient support, he can win through a transparent vote. He does not need to be carried into office under a manufactured consensus.

The OIF’s rules provide for consensus, but they also permit a vote when consensus cannot be reached. Its 53 full members are therefore capable of deciding the matter openly.

This is now about more than Cioloș, Mushikiwabo, Lumumba or Bâ. It is a test of whether African Union decisions carry any weight when European interests enter the room.

The DRC has every sovereign right to support the candidate of its choice. But it cannot reasonably withdraw its African candidate, disregard an African Union position, embrace a European contender and then demand that the rest of Africa call the arrangement “consensus.”

Romanian mercenaries came to Congo with weapons and left through Rwanda after their mission collapsed. A Romanian politician has now arrived through diplomacy, carried by Kinshasa’s support.

This time, Africa is being asked to surrender its position without a single shot being fired.

The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power.

The party has also pledged to develop new guidelines so that laptops and tablets are not the "default in classrooms".

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott cited recent warnings from clinicians that excessive screen time could be damaging children's health, adding that "everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards".

The government is currently developing new screen-time guidance for children and has previously said it would consult on the safety of AI in schools.

The vast majority of school exams in the UK are pen and paper based. Under the previous government led by Sir Keir Starmer, exam regulator Ofqual launched a consultation last year , external on the introduction of on-screen exams.

But it emphasised that pen and paper would "remain central" and that the most widely taken subjects would not be moving to digital assessments for the "foreseeable future".

In their announcement on Sunday, the Tories said they would "put a stop" to the introduction of screen-based exams, and require screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day.

The party said it would also minimise the amount of coursework in school assessments to avoid lowering educational standards "by allowing children to become overly reliant on the use of generative AI platforms".

Under the plans, primary schools would be required to keep screen use to a minimum and only use screens where necessary, such as in computing lessons.

Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under stricter rules for schools in England

Ministers to issue guidance on children's screen use

The announcement comes after a group of more than 150 clinicians warned last month that the amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health" .

An open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper from the clinicians said they were prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools".

Trott said: "I want to slash screen use in classrooms and set a new norm where screens are no longer the default. That means no screens in early years, minimal use in primary schools except where required by the curriculum."

Figures from the most recent government survey , external show that in 2024, most teachers (89%) used interactive whiteboards within lessons. But the survey also found that most teachers - 79% in primary and 69% in secondary - said pupils were using individual devices in fewer than a quater of lessons, or not at all.

The Tories said their plans draw on the work of the Health Professionals for Safer Screens campaign group, which has warned about the effects of excessive screen time on children.

Its founder Dr Rebecca Foljambe said: "We have become excessively preoccupied with why children are on screens. Although content is important, this distracts from the fact that daily screen time can profoundly affect a child's health, whatever they are watching or doing."

As part of its proposal, the Tories said £900m that "the government currently spends on EdTech" would be repurposed to create a £250m fund for new textbooks.

A Department for Education spokesperson said schools decided how much to spend on educational technology, which alongside screens also included things such as management information systems, from within their own budgets.

"It is up to schools to decide how they use their funding in the best interests of pupils," they said.

They added: "Building on the guidance we have published for children under 5, in the new year the department will publish clear guidance on screen use for all children aged 5 to 18, giving parents the advice they need."

A ban on smartphones in schools in England came into force in June, making individual schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.

Education is a devolved matter in the UK, with each of the four nations managing their own systems.

The UK social media ban for under-16s - banning children from major platforms such as TikTok and Instagram - will come into force in March.

As an ambassador for young carers, raising awareness is important to Neraya

Neraya is only 15 but cannot remember a time when she was not a carer for her two sisters.

She is among the young carers crying out for what they have called crucial support, with Neraya saying she has even had to explain what she does to her teachers.

On Monday, the Welsh government will publish a national strategy for unpaid carers, which will have seven priorities including earlier recognition and mental health support.

Neraya, from Bridgend, said people in her position wanted the chance of "a childhood of our own".

Carers Wales said the strategy looked positive in parts, but it was "disappointed" manifesto promises would be excluded and raised questions over how it will be funded.

There are an estimated 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK , external , 170,000 of whom are young.

The 2021 Census said this included about 120,000 carers, aged five to 17 in England and 8,200 in Wales.

Scottish government recognised there were 42,050 unpaid carers identified in the 2021-22 Carers Census.

Neraya's sisters have varying needs and she helps with practical things such as helping them get ready for school, as well as emotional support, and said there was a lack of understanding about the sacrifices young carers make.

"There's not the understanding that you might not have been able to go somewhere because we had some sort of problem within the household because my sister was ill and I'm worrying about my sister, that kind of thing," she said.

Neraya said she used to get "picked on" because people did not know what was happening with her siblings and others tended to assume they were just "naughty".

Once, in primary school, she said she was called to stand in front of her class and explain what she did because "teachers themselves didn't understand what it was".

Being a carer does not take away from her life, she said, but having support and being made to feel "valid" would give people like her "the chance to have a... childhood of our own at the same time".

The Welsh government said its strategy would focus on seven priority areas, shaped by conversations with carers with the aim of improving early recognition, access to support and respite, and better information on their rights.

It also indicated more support for mental health and wellbeing.

Reece says support with helping build CVs and fun trips help young carers

Reece Peachy, 17, from Ebbw Vale, Blaenau Gwent, helps care for his youngest brother while his parents support his other siblings with additional needs.

He said being a carer was "difficult but easy at the same time", but has to be home more than the average teenager.

He said: "If I have plans me and my mam will talk about it and I'll watch him. You naturally just help them out and I've been doing it for so long its just an instinct."

Reece said it could be "tough sometimes" as he balances his responsibilities with seeing friends and going to college as he puts his brother "before anything else".

"It can feel very frustrating and lonely because I wont spend much time with other people and sometimes I have to push aside things I want to do."

He said his local young carers group helped a lot by providing trips around Wales and helping him get his Duke of Edinburgh award to add to his CV.

He plans to finish his college course in carpentry before doing an apprenticeship, all while continuing to help his parents.

"I know if I move away too far they will struggle. My parents always say they are so grateful for what I do."

Cerys Morgan wants to see more support for carers under 10 who might not understand what their role is

Cerys Morgan, 19, has helped support her 16-year-old brother, who is non-verbal and autistic, as well as being physically disabled, since she was eight.

She helps with mostly physical tasks - such as getting him ready for school and taking his medication - but also provides emotional support.

"I've developed an understanding more than I think other people would as a sister," she said.

"I understand how he's feeling, what his needs are and how I can support him if he's having a hard day or a happy day and know what's best for him, in that way as being a sister, to support him."

She called emotional support for young carers "really important" in order to help them develop skills and resilience in their roles, especially those who find themselves in the role at a young age.

"When I was eight I didn't understand what a young carer meant," she said.

She suggested the Welsh government could look at mentor schemes to link young people up - something she wished she had "when I was little to support me and for me to communicate with as well".

Deputy minister for social care, Delyth Jewell, described unpaid carers as the "backbone of care" across Wales.

But Carers Wales said the strategy does not go far enough.

Head of external affairs Rob Simkins said: "There are some welcome parts of the new strategy, particularly around access to respite care and a desire to see more carers receiving support.

"However, it is not clear how the government intends to make the step-change needed without additional investment to provide the extra support that unpaid carers desperately need.

"It is also disappointing that the manifesto commitment to ensuring carers' needs assessments , external are completed within 28 days is missing from the strategy."

He said the organisation wanted to make sure unpaid carers lives are better and was not sure that this strategy "will go as far as we want it to".

The Welsh government said: "We have engaged extensively with a wide range of social care groups and our national strategy for unpaid carers will help ensure they get the recognition and support they deserve.

"We are considering whether changes are needed to strengthen support for carers, including imposing a timescale on the completion of carers' needs assessments."

The UK will have a "voice in the room" but no vote on European Union food policies as part of a so-called "Brexit reset" to reduce red tape, EU relations minister Hamish Falconer has told the BBC.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham hopes to agree a deal at a summit on Friday but critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker" but not a rule maker.

Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules and said the deal could help bring down prices for shoppers.

The reset would not involve any upfront payments, Falconer added, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

Falconer said it was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

In September, the Conservative Party said it was "raising the alarm" over the government's planned reset, saying it would leave British consumers and businesses "dangerously exposed, with no input on how regulations are made or power to reject them".

Both the Conservatives and Reform have said they would undo the planned reset if they were in power.

Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer

The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.

Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said the deal would help bring down costs for firms importing food.

"This will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves," he said.

He said currently "pages and pages" of form-filling meant some suppliers had given up exporting to the EU and some products, such as Lincolnshire sausages, meant they were almost impossible to export at all.

Some M&S trucks require over 300 pages of documents for food exports, from export health certificates, phytosanitary certificates, visits from vets and border check paperwork.

Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.

"The amount of paperwork you would need to do, the amount of uncertainty - you have to have it in the right pen colour, if it's not black, it might be refused," Falconer said.

"If you're selling Cox apples from Kent, they have to wait a day before they go into the European Union."

The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.

Falconer said the impact of the reset deal for food would be an additional £5bn.

The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.

This wider agreement includes aligning emissions trading rules, and agreeing to a youth mobility scheme, as well as the reset on food trading.

Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU

Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.

Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.

But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.

He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.

UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.

Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.

Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.

He said there were bound to be compromises and trade-offs in any deal but that where the UK had advantages the government wanted to make sure "those aren't lost under the deal".

Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.

"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.

Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.

Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.

"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill

National Insurance (NI) paid by businesses on workers aged under 25 should be gradually lowered to encourage companies to create jobs for young people, a major review of youth unemployment will say.

A report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will suggest the government should reduce NI costs over five years for people aged between 21 and 24 years old, starting in retail and hospitality.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms. Milburn will say the number of young people not in employment, education or training - known as Neets - was not started by the NI rise.

But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".

The independent report, which has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday, will also make recommendations on reducing the UK's benefits bill.

Milburn has said the government spends £22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive. There are nearly one million so-called Neets aged between 16 and 24 in the UK, according to data from the Office for National Statistics.

He will recommend that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Milburn wants the government to provide a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support . Those who refuse to take up help could lose their benefits.

Milburn is also expected to say that helping young people develop skills is pointless if there are no jobs available for them.

The former health secretary will recommend doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.

But he will say this should only be done "when fiscal conditions allow".

Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.

Milburn is set to say that given the UK's fiscal position, an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.

But Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns three salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and the minimum wage.

She said she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any. Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff.

Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads".

Salon-owner Collette Osborne says she is "inundated" with CVs from young people

She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages.

"I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said.

Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters.

"I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs."

Milburn told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme he agreed with a recent move by Chancellor John Healey to slow down the equalisation of the national minimum wage across age groups.

Labour had pledged in its manifesto to remove "discriminatory age bands" and close the gap between adult minimum wages and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.

But in his Budget, Healey said pay for that age group would rise from £10.85 to £11.27 an hour in April next year while people aged 21 and over will see their wages increase from £12.71 to £13.21.

"I understand why because nobody wants to see young workers on poverty pay," Milburn said, but he said it "imposed a lot of costs on [the] government".

"I think we have got to look very carefully at the convergence issue," he said.

Milburn said he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers.

"Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said.

"The state has a responsibility to help them with that."

On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit.

People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales.

McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029".

But Whately said it is "just absurd that they are taxing businesses here and they're going to subsidise things that look like jobs over here. Just stop doing the taxing".

She said the Tories want to halve employer NI costs "because I talk to businesses who say they really want to employ young people but they just can't afford to anymore and the regulation that the Labour Party has put in place has made it harder".

Milburn will say that if the government does go ahead with a gradual reduction in NI over five years, it should start with businesses such as shops, bars and restaurants.

Retail and hospitality together provide 37% of jobs for young people aged between 16 and 24.

Some 106,000 people from a wide range of groups took to the streets in France on Saturday, including 24,000 in Paris

Police in Paris have issued a five-day ban on protests near 10 secondary schools and five universities as authorities try to control weeks of blockades and violence at educational venues in France.

The order prohibits unauthorised gatherings or marches within 100m of the sites from 16 to 20 November.

Paris police chief Patrice Faure said the ban was necessary due to "numerous disruptions and blockades around certain secondary schools and establishments of higher learning" and "persistent violence".

A wave of protests began in France September over poor secondary school conditions, before spreading to universities, workers and a "yellow-vest" movement against the cost of living.

Announcing the order, the Paris police chief said blockades around certain secondary schools and universities have led to damaged public property, violence against members of the educational community and clashes with law enforcement.

Mayors of eight Parisian districts had contacted the regional education authority to call for measures to "secure the entrances and exits" of blockaded secondary schools, local media report.

Some 1,548 people have been arrested in Paris since the start of the protests, Faure said on Sunday.

Riot police clash with demonstrators in Paris on Saturday

On Saturday, 106,000 people from a range of groups took to the streets in France, including 24,000 in Paris, the interior ministry said.

It marked the fifth Saturday in a row where students, unions and yellow-vest activists went out to protest.

The number of protesters was much lower than previously, and so was the number of those arrested, the ministry said - 219 across the country, including 45 in Paris.
